kp.k: Study links filing trends, complaint text, and outcomes
kp.d: Cohen-Sasson analyzes approximately 2.8 million original federal civil filings from the Federal Judicial Center for FY2008–FY2025, excluding prisoner petitions and unknown case types. November 30, 2022 is the GenAI cutoff. The complaint analysis covers 12,842 CourtListener pro se complaints from FY2018–FY2025 in Civil Rights and Other Statutory cases; 12,451 match FJC records, comprising 7,284 pre-AI and 5,167 post-AI cases. The design identifies associations rather than causal effects and does not directly observe litigants' AI use.
qs: The design is descriptive and associational:
The paper does not observe individual GenAI use;

kp.k: Federal self-representation increased sharply after the GenAI cutoff
kp.d: The plaintiff pro se rate increased from 11.33% to 16.94%, a 5.61 percentage-point or 49.5% relative increase (p<0.001). Comparing the last four pre-AI quarters with the last four post-AI quarters gives 13.06% versus 19.59%; FY2025-Q4 reached 22.30%. Average quarterly pro se filings increased from 4,152 to 6,423 (+54.7%), while total filings increased 2.9% and represented filings declined 3.2%. The author therefore identifies increased self-represented filing volume, not simply general docket expansion.

kp.k: Models identify acceleration, not an immediate causal AI effect
kp.d: Interrupted time-series analysis estimates a statistically insignificant immediate level shift of +1.090 percentage points (p=0.171), but a significant post-AI slope change of +0.729 percentage points per quarter (p<0.001), or +0.727 with COVID controls. District- and case-category-adjusted logistic regression estimates OR=1.364, 95% CI [1.351, 1.377]; adding a COVID FY2020 control gives OR=1.352, 95% CI [1.339, 1.366]. These checks support an unusual post-cutoff acceleration, not identification of GenAI as its cause. Gradual technological diffusion is offered as a compatible interpretation.
qs: Acceleration, not a One-time Level Shift

kp.k: Changes vary substantially across civil case categories
kp.d: Other Statutory pro se rates rose from 11.23% to 19.51% (+8.28 percentage points), and Civil Rights from 28.16% to 35.60% (+7.44). Together these categories represent approximately 36.7% of all-civil filings and motivate the complaint-level focus. Intellectual Property changed little (+0.14, p=0.064), while Social Security and Immigration declined by 2.31 and 3.73 points. Differences in stakes, specialization, counsel availability, and costs are proposed explanations rather than tested mechanisms.
qs: Other Statutory cases show the largest
These explanations are suggestive rather than exhaustive;

kp.k: Filing counts do not establish lawyer displacement
kp.d: Although represented filings declined slightly overall, the author finds no clear displacement evidence: both represented and pro se filings increased in Civil Rights, and the represented-filing decline in Other Statutory began before the GenAI cutoff. Increased self-representation therefore cannot simply be interpreted as AI replacing retained lawyers.

kp.k: Textual proxy indicates increased AI-consistent complaint drafting
kp.d: The proxy averages direction-adjusted ranks for sentence-length variability, AI-marker vocabulary density, and moving-average type-token ratio. A score above 2.25 flags a complaint, calibrated against pre-AI high-scoring text. The reported net post-AI increase is 13.9% for non-form complaints, 9.8% pooled, and 4.3% for form complaints. Forms serve as a quasi-control, not a no-AI control, because templates can obscure assistance. These estimates concern visible drafting signatures, not verified AI adoption or total AI use.

kp.k: Proxy checks support plausibility without validating individual use
kp.d: Quarterly non-form flagging correlates with ChatGPT weekly active users (Spearman ρ=+0.936, n=11) and Google Trends interest in AI (ρ=+0.944, n=12). Component indicators move in expected directions, and joint high-score co-occurrence rises from 2.08% to 8.31%; the observed-versus-independence multiplier increases from 1.33 to 2.60. Alternative thresholds retain positive net increases: +15.4% above 2.00 and +10.3% above 2.50. The author presents these as credibility checks, not direct evidence of individual use.

kp.k: Flagged non-form complaints contain more legal citations
kp.d: Median citations per 1,000 words are 6.01 for post-AI flagged non-form complaints, versus 3.98 for all pre-AI non-form complaints (+51.1%, p<0.0001) and 4.40 for post-AI unflagged complaints (+36.6%, p<0.0001). This supports a finding of greater citation richness, not better legal merit or citation accuracy. Form complaints show the opposite pattern: flagged complaints have median density 4.44 versus 5.08 pre-AI and 5.79 post-AI unflagged.
qs: Form complaints do not show the same citation-density

kp.k: Flagged complaints disproportionately involve newly observed plaintiffs
kp.d: In the linked post-AI non-form sample, 79.4% of flagged complaints involve observed first-time filers versus 70.2% of unflagged complaints, reported as +9.3 percentage points (OR=1.638, 95% CI [1.280, 2.097], p<0.001). This weakens an exclusively serial-litigator explanation. First-time status means the normalized primary-plaintiff name's first appearance in the focal sample, not proof of no previous litigation elsewhere.
qs: not proof that the person had never filed elsewhere.

kp.k: Financial and gender findings qualify democratization claims
kp.d: Fee-waiver status appears in 27.3% of flagged versus 24.4% of unflagged post-AI non-form complaints (p=0.12), while population-level pro se fee-waiver rates decline from 42.3% to 35.9%. The study does not find concentration among financially constrained litigants. Among binary-classified names at NamSor's >=0.80 threshold, inferred-female shares are 19.7% versus 15.0%, reported as +4.6 percentage points (p=0.051). The gender result is suggestive, name-inferred rather than self-reported, and marginal under both tested classification thresholds.
qs: suggestive rather than conclusive evidence of gender

kp.d: Post-AI linked non-form flag rates are highest in the Tenth Circuit (33.3%), Fourth (30.0%), First (29.3%), D.C. (29.1%), and Eleventh (24.7%), compared with 14.9% in the Ninth and 15.5% in the Sixth. The circuit concentration test is significant (χ²=55.319, df=11, p<0.001, Cramér's V=0.132), supporting uneven distribution rather than uniform diffusion.

kp.k: Flagged cases face more dismissal and earlier termination
kp.d: Among terminated post-AI non-form cases, flagged complaints have dismissal rates of 61.1% versus 53.6% (+7.5 percentage points, p=0.006). Dismissals comprise Want of Prosecution, Lack of Jurisdiction, and Other Dismissal, excluding settlements and voluntary dismissals; the gap is mainly in Other Dismissal. Termination before issue is joined occurs in 47.78% versus 39.04% (+8.75 points, FDR-adjusted p=0.002). These procedural codes identify the stage of termination rather than elapsed duration.

kp.k: No demonstrated win-rate advantage; outcome follow-up remains limited
kp.d: The primary non-form plaintiff win rate is 6.4% for flagged versus 8.4% for unflagged complaints (p=0.635); pooled rates are 3.7% versus 5.3% (p=0.525). The denominator includes only clearly coded plaintiff or defendant judgments, with 47 flagged and 333 unflagged cases in the primary comparison. Rare wins and nonsignificant differences support neither improvement nor worsening of win rates. The broader post-AI terminated-case working set is n=3,924; pending cases create right-censoring and potential overrepresentation of early terminations.
qs: Plaintiff wins are relatively rare in the pro se data.

kp.k: Drafting access differs from access to effective remedies
kp.d: The author interprets the findings as a distinction between easier court entry and substantive legal efficacy: more citation-rich complaints do not show improved outcomes. Nevertheless, participation can have democratic, dignitary, and procedural-justice value independent of winning. The paper also proposes, conditionally, that more filings at stable favorable-judgment rates could produce more successful outcomes in absolute terms; this is not an established causal finding.
qs: Access to Justice or Access to Drafting?
Win rates and filing volumes are distinct quantities.

kp.k: Proposed mechanisms include superficial drafting and weaker case selection
kp.d: The discussion offers three explanations that the design cannot distinguish: AI may improve formal presentation without producing fact-specific plausible claims; lower drafting costs may admit marginal, premature, jurisdictionally defective, or weak cases; and sycophancy may reinforce litigants' confidence in questionable claims. These are hypotheses, not measured mechanisms or evidence that particular litigants knowingly filed weak cases.
qs: One possible explanation is surface-level assistance.
cannot be separated with this study’s design;

kp.k: Court adaptation is recommended over restricting litigants
kp.d: The author warns that rapid public adoption may outpace courts' capacity for threshold review because courts face procurement, ethics, and reliability constraints. This capacity mismatch is an institutional interpretation rather than a directly measured workload effect. The paper favors staff training, triage, AI-assisted filing policies, and careful evaluation of court-side tools rather than prohibiting litigants' AI use. It recommends longer outcome follow-up, direct litigant-side validation, mechanism-specific research, and extension to pro se defendants and state courts.
qs: The broader issue is asymmetric adaptation.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Cohen-Sasson argues that widespread public GenAI access is associated with increased federal civil self-representation and expanded drafting capacity, but not demonstrably better litigation success or clear lawyer displacement.
pts.d: The author reports that the federal civil plaintiff pro se rate increased from 11.33% before the GenAI cutoff to 16.94% afterward, with an accelerating trend rather than a statistically significant immediate level shift. The increase varies by case category and is particularly pronounced in Civil Rights and Other Statutory cases. In the complaint-text analysis, the net increase above the pre-AI baseline in AI-flagged non-form complaints is 13.9%; this is a measure of visible AI-consistent drafting, not verified individual use. Flagged non-form complaints are more citation-dense, but terminated cases have higher dismissal rates and more early-stage terminations, without a statistically significant win-rate difference. The author distinguishes expanded access to drafting from effective access to remedies, while recognizing participation as potentially valuable in itself. Conditionally, more filings could produce more favorable judgments in absolute numbers even without improved per-case success. Proposed explanations for the outcome pattern include superficial legal formality, entry of weaker or defective claims as drafting barriers fall, and sycophancy-reinforced overconfidence; the study does not distinguish these mechanisms. The author finds no clear evidence of lawyer displacement from filing counts. The institutional prediction is that public adoption by litigants can change courts without formal court adoption of AI and could generate a capacity mismatch if drafting expands faster than court screening capacity. The recommended response is court-side adaptation rather than prohibiting litigant AI use.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source offers large-scale observational filing data and a linked complaint-text analysis, supplemented by robustness checks and literature-based interpretations rather than causal identification.
pts.d: Cohen-Sasson analyzes approximately 2.8 million original federal civil filings from the Federal Judicial Center, excluding prisoner petitions and unknown case types. The complaint sample contains 12,842 CourtListener complaints in Civil Rights and Other Statutory cases; 12,451 link to FJC metadata. Filing evidence includes pre/post comparisons, quarterly trends, interrupted time-series models, and district-, case-category-, and COVID-adjusted analyses. Average quarterly pro se filings increase from 4,152 to 6,423, while represented filings decline modestly from 31,654 to 30,637; Civil Rights represented filings also rise, and the represented decline in Other Statutory cases predates the cutoff. The AI-consistent drafting proxy combines sentence-length variability, AI-marker vocabulary density, and moving-average type-token ratio, with a threshold calibrated against the pre-AI baseline. Credibility checks examine correlations with public GenAI adoption and attention, component movement, indicator co-occurrence, and alternative thresholds. These are proxy checks, not ground-truth verification of litigants' AI use. Among post-AI non-form complaints, median citation density is 6.01 for flagged versus 4.40 for unflagged complaints. Among terminated non-form cases, dismissal rates are 61.1% versus 53.6% (p=0.006), and termination before issue is joined occurs in 47.78% versus 39.04%. Win rates among clearly judgment-coded non-form cases are 6.4% versus 8.4% (p=0.635); the author does not infer either improved or worsened win rates. Court-capacity mismatch and the proposed explanations for litigation outcomes are interpretive arguments, not separately measured causal findings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings cover the period through FY2025, using the November 30, 2022 ChatGPT release as the cutoff; AI attribution, outcome completeness, and generalizability are explicitly qualified.
pts.d: The macro filing analysis covers FY2008–FY2025; complaint texts cover FY2018–FY2025. Cases are assigned to periods by filing date, with November 30, 2022 marking public GenAI availability and FY2023-Q1 treated as a mixed transition quarter in quarterly analysis. By FY2025-Q4, the pro se filing share reaches 22.30%. The author explicitly describes the study as descriptive and associational, not causal. Complaint-level findings concern two selected federal case categories, especially freely drafted non-form complaints, and should not be extended automatically to all federal litigation or state courts. Form complaints serve as a quasi-control because templates can obscure AI assistance; they are not presumed AI-free. The proxy captures visible drafting signatures and may miss brainstorming, translation, research, or light editing. Outcome analyses include only terminated cases and are subject to right-censoring because many recent cases remain pending. Observed first-time status means first appearance of a normalized primary-plaintiff name within the focal sample, not first-ever litigation. Gender is inferred from names rather than self-reported, and the observed female-share difference is marginal. Predictions about absolute numbers of successful claims depend on expanded filings alongside stable favorable-judgment rates; institutional capacity concerns depend on litigant adoption outpacing court adaptation. No quantified future forecast is supplied.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are self-represented federal civil plaintiffs and courts; the reported changes are uneven across case categories, filer groups, financial-constraint measures, and geography.
pts.d: The study's strongest macro increases occur in Other Statutory cases, from 11.23% to 19.51%, and Civil Rights cases, from 28.16% to 35.60%. Other categories show smaller increases, little movement, or declines, including Social Security and Immigration. In the linked post-AI non-form sample, 79.4% of flagged complaints versus 70.2% of unflagged complaints are associated with observed first-time filers, which the author interprets as inconsistent with a purely serial-filer account. The name-inferred female share is modestly higher among flagged complaints, 19.7% versus 15.0%, but the result is suggestive rather than conclusive. Fee-waiver status is not significantly associated with flagging: 27.3% versus 24.4%, p=0.12. The overall pro se fee-waiver share falls from 42.3% to 35.9%; accordingly, the author does not characterize AI-consistent drafting as primarily benefiting indigent litigants. AI-flag rates vary across circuits, with higher rates in the Tenth, Fourth, First, D.C., and Eleventh Circuits and lower rates in the Ninth and Sixth. Courts may face more threshold screening work as complaints become easier to produce, while procurement, ethics, and reliability constraints may slow institutional adaptation. Suggested responses include staff training, triage, filing policies, and evaluation of court-side tools. Lawyers are affected only indirectly in this study: the source does not establish displacement or quantify employment or revenue effects.
